name: Malimiut Iñupiaq
confidence_why: Lanz 2010, the only first-hand study of Malimiut Iñupiaq prosody, states that no rule for the placement of word prominence has been established and that the basic prosodic type is still open, Kaplan's phonology of North Alaskan Iñupiaq (1979, 1981) is does not discuss stress and his comparative statements (1985, 2001) say only that Inuit lacks the Yupik rhythmic stress, and the sole contrary remark, a second-hand "no prosody at all" attributed to Jacobson through Kaplan 1994b, is rejected by Lanz's own phonetic measurements, so the classification "undetermined" rests on one modern source with nothing real against it.
catalog_citation: Lanz, Linda A. 2010. A grammar of Iñupiaq morphosyntax. PhD dissertation, Rice University, Houston. xiv+260 pp. (Malimiut Coastal dialect, Noatak/Kotzebue Sound area.) ANLA IN010L2010; Rice repository hdl 1911/62097.
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 'Phonetics and phonology', sec. 2.7 'Stress' pp. 42-46, incl. sec. 2.7.2 'Stress/syllable prominence in Iñupiaq' pp. 45-46.
catalog_quote: Surprisingly, there are no previously published studies of Iñupiaq prosody, including stress or lack thereof. ... Furthermore, Kaplan (1994b) cites S. Jacobson (undated), saying Iñupiaq has no prosody at all, a dubious and typologically unlikely claim. Listening to Iñupiaq, there is an intuitive sense that at least one syllable per word is more prominent than any others; whether this syllable prominence is lexical stress or not remains to be seen, as there is no a priori reason to assume that lexical stress is a salient feature of Iñupiaq. Furthermore, it may be prosodically motivated or morphologically motivated prominence (cf. Tuttle (2000:35–36) for Apache). I will use SYLLABLE PROMINENCE and STRESS interchangeably here and leave the status of stress as a possible meaning-bearing unit in Iñupiaq for later study. [p. 45] Rules for the placement of syllable prominence were not a priority; however, as Kaplan (2001) mentions that Iñupiaq does not have rhythmic stress or lengthening like Yup’ik does, any evidence that supports or contradicts his findings would be of interest. ... [p. 46] In summary, we know that duration is not likely to be important in Malimiut Iñupiaq stress/syllable prominence, and that rhythmic lengthening is not happening. ... More work is necessary to solve the dilemma of basic prosodic type in Iñupiaq as well as other Inuit languages/dialects.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (image-only Acrobat Paper Capture scan, 275 pp., no text). I rendered pp. 57, 60, 61 (= printed pp. 42, 45, 46) to PNG and read them directly, and compared with the saved scanned. All three quoted segments are on the pages stated and are verbatim: p.42 sec. 2.7 'Stress' opens 'Surprisingly, there are no previously published studies of Inupiaq prosody, including stress or lack thereof.' and later 'Listening to Inupiaq, there is an intuitive sense that at least one syllable per word is more prominent than any others; whether this syllable prominence is lexical stress or not remains to be seen, as there is no a priori reason to assume that lexical stress is a salient feature of I…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand treatment states that Malimiut (North Alaskan) Iñupiaq words have one perceptually prominent syllable, but the author explicitly leaves open whether this is lexical stress and gives no rule for its location; acoustically the prominence is cued by F0, intensity, loudness and spectral tilt, not duration; there is no Yupik-style rhythmic (alternating) stress or iambic lengthening. Kaplan (2001, quoted ibid.) says rhythmic stress systems are absent from Inuit; Kaplan 1981's NAI phonology has no stress section and equates English stress with Iñupiaq vowel length in loans.
new_statements.exceptions: None; author notes Kaplan (1994b, after Jacobson) claimed Iñupiaq 'has no prosody at all', which she rejects as typologically unlikely.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level perceptual 'syllable prominence' in elicited Malimiut Coastal (Kotzebue area) speech, based on the author's unpublished 2008 acoustic study; placement (word vs phrase, citation forms) not analysed.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Lanz 2010) describes the Malimiut Coastal dialect (Kotzebue Sound Inupiatun, Glottolog kotz1238, under Malimiutun mali1289, a dialect of nort2943). The other NAI descriptions examined (Kaplan 1979/1981, MacLean 1993/2012, Nagai 2006) cover Barrow/North Slope (nort2944) and Kobuk (kobu1239) and are silent on stress. Kaplan 1985's explicit stress rule (non-final closed syllables and long vowels stressed) is for King Island / Seward Peninsula Inupiaq, a different Glottolog language (nort2945, Bering Strait dialect king1259), not nort2943.

sources.note: Sec. 2.7 'Stress' (pp.42-46): no prior published study of Inupiaq prosody; perceptually at least one syllable per word is more prominent but whether this is lexical stress is undetermined; placement rules not established; her phonetic study (Lanz 2008) found F0, intensity, loudness, spectral tilt significant cues, duration not; no Yupik-type rhythmic lengthening; cites Kaplan (2001) that rhythmic stress systems are absent from Inuit and Kaplan (1994b, citing Jacobson) that Inupiaq 'has no prosody at all' (which she calls dubious).
